intro: The third movement of the String Quartet in C major, Op. 54 No. 2, Hob. III:57, is a C major minuet that follows directly on the end of the Adagio. In the C minor Trio all four players share one melody before dividing into chords.

sections.label: A · Menuetto in C major
sections.mNote: First-violin melody, ending on a rising scale.

sections.label: B · Trio, C minor, four instruments
sections.mNote: The Trio opens with a unison melody.

sections.label: A′ · Menuetto in C major, da capo
sections.mNote: The minuet is repeated da capo after the Trio.

cues.title: Minuet in C major, attacca
cues.text: Haydn joins the Adagio to this C major minuet without a pause. After the violin line of the slow movement, the four players begin a dance marked Allegretto.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 190–191: attacca followed by Menuetto, Allegretto. Laurie Shulman discusses the connection: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trio in C minor
cues.text: The Trio turns to C minor, the Adagio’s key. All four instruments play the same melody in unison, and augmented chords intervene.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 192. Shulman identifies the C minor Trio, unison melody and augmented chords. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Precedent in Op. 20 No. 2
cues.text: Haydn had already linked a slow movement and minuet this closely in the C major Quartet, Op. 20 No. 2. Here the Trio also takes up the Adagio’s C minor, so material from the earlier movement returns within the dance.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman names Op. 20 No. 2 as the precedent and describes the links between this Trio and the Adagio. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Return of the minuet
cues.text: Menuetto da capo sends the quartet back to the beginning. The minuet returns in C major, with the first violin leading. It ends with its rising scale and final chords.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192: Menuetto D.C. at the end of the Trio; the Menuetto’s rising scales and Fine.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Finale: Adagio, Presto, Adagio
cues.text: The finale is a second Adagio, with a Presto in its middle. Laurie Shulman wrote that the two slow movements shift “the entire balance and emotional weight” of the quartet.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, programme note for the Schumann Quartet, 20 November 2022, p. 2, on the finale (Adagio, Presto, Adagio). https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

transitions.title: Rising scales, then the C minor Trio
transitions.to: B · Trio, C minor, four instruments
transitions.how: Rising scales carry all four instruments to the minuet’s fortissimo close in C major. The Trio changes the key signature to three flats and begins in C minor, with all four players sharing the melody. The cello plays the tune with the others and has no separate bass line.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192; Shulman’s description of the unison C minor Trio. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

transitions.title: Trio returns to the Menuetto
transitions.from: B · Trio, C minor, four instruments
transitions.to: A′ · Menuetto in C major, da capo
transitions.how: The Trio ends in C minor. The direction Menuetto D.C. sends the players straight back to the C major opening. The first violin takes the tune again, and the other three resume their accompaniment. The rising scales now lead to the Fine and the end of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192: the Trio’s close and da capo direction, returning to the Menuetto and its Fine.

source.title: Haydn, String Quartet in C major, Op. 54 No. 2, score (Leipzig: Eulenburg, ed. Wilhelm Altmann)
source.locator: Menuetto and Trio, printed pp. 191–192: C major dance, C minor Trio and da capo.

timeline.note: The first violin leads the C major minuet above the other three players’ chords.
The C minor Trio brings all four players together on one melody.
Da capo: the first violin plays the minuet’s opening tune again.

composer.epithet: Composer known for an orchestral work in which the players leave one at a time, and for a quartet that continues after listeners think it has ended.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
